- When sentiment is consistently negative (0.00 or low), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive pessimism.  
- After a sharp price spike, model often overshoots and fails to correct — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), model frequently underestimates mean reversion — increase forecast toward historical mean or recent 7-day average.  
- When sentiment is strongly positive (1.00 or 0.67), model often overestimates future price — cap forecast at 10–15% above recent high or adjust downward if sentiment drops within 3 days.  
- Model tends to lag in early periods (first 5–7 days) — increase forecast slightly for first 3–5 days if sentiment is positive or neutral.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated low values, model underestimates volatility — add 2–3% volatility buffer to forecast range.  
- Avoid forecasting extreme values (e.g., >100 or <80) unless sentiment strongly supports it — use sentiment as a filter for outlier rejection.
